transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-01
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Priya Sharma (Redwood SE), Evan Lopez (Redwood CSM), Alex Martinez (FinSettle ML Infra), Rita Chen (Eng Manager), Samir Gupta (Security Architect), Leah Kim (Product)

Summary: Quick review of POC caching metrics, discussed prompt reuse strategy and canonicalization, agreed on next benchmark matrix (10k prefixes, multiple TTLs), and security/docation follow-ups. Some verbal transcription noise in places.

Topics: prefix cache hit rates; KV cache performance; TTL tradeoffs; prompt normalization/hash keys; memory/eviction policies; integration next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll run about 45 minutes and leave some time for q's, um quick check in, is this still a good agenda?
[00:12] Rita: yes works for me, thanks Jordan
[00:16] Alex: good here, also want to get into the TTL tradeoffs this time
[00:22] Priya: awesome, i'll pull up the latest numbers we ran overnight, so TLDR: baseline without caching our p50 token latency is ~240ms, with prefix/KV cache hit we're seeing p50 drop to ~62ms on hits, and overall token cost down by 28% so far but hit rate is the thing.
[00:45] Samir: can you repeat the hit-rate numbers? i think last week you said low 40s?
[00:52] Priya: yeah baseline we had 42% prefix match-ish when we used naive template matching, after we applied normalization + trimming of user metadata we bumped to 64% for the repeat-transaction flows - so that's the 64% number on our staging replay. note that real prod mix may be lower cause of more varied prompts.
[01:18] Alex: the 64% is promising, question about distribution: are most hits concentrated in the top 500 prefixes or is it long tail?
[01:27] Priya: good q, it's a heavy head: top 500 prefixes account for ~52% of hits, top 2k prefixes about 77%, then long tail. so caching those top prefixes gives outsized wins.
[01:43] Rita: that suggests we can start with a hot-set pinning approach on dedicated pools - can we pin top keys?
[01:50] Priya: yes we can mark hot keys to avoid eviction in the in-memory cache; on Redwood Dedicated you can configure reserved cache memory and pinning policy. small note: pinning increases memory footprint and reduces ability to cache other ephemeral keys.
[02:06] Leah: any observations about cold-start latency for new prefixes?
[02:10] Priya: cold starts are still the slow path, p95 on misses is about 380-430ms depending on seq len, we saw a few outliers where a big template plus lots of metadata pushed generation to 700ms. that's why canonicalization matters.
[02:26] Jordan: quick thing on methodology - we ran two replays: one that mirrors prod 30-day traffic (sampled) and a second A/B where we applied prompt normalization and aggressive trimming. The A/B bumped hit-rate from 42 to 64 and dropped token costs by 18% on that workload.
[02:48] Samir: on security front, how do you handle keying and KMS for KV cache identifiers? we need to ensure keys aren't leaking PHI in cache keys.
[02:58] Priya: good catch - we recommend hashing canonical prompts with a keyed HMAC (customer KMS) so the cache key is an opaque digest; Redwood supports customer-managed keys via KMS for HMAC signing of keys in Private and Dedicated. in Hosted mode we support per-tenant keying with envelope encryption. there may be slight perf overhead but it's small.
[03:20] Samir: does that mean we need to change our code to call KMS on every request?
[03:24] Priya: no, not on every request - typically you derive the key for the service at startup and perform HMAC locally; only rotate/refresh per policy. we can doc the flow.
[03:33] Alex: about TTLs - we tried 30s in the first run and hit-rate looked ok but we were worried about stale info for dynamic fields. what did you try?
[03:41] Priya: we ran 5s, 30s, 120s TTLs. 5s gave lower hit-rate (about -8% vs 30s) but minimized staleness for dynamic attributes; 120s gave marginally higher hit-rate ~+6% vs 30s but increased risk for stale dynamic data. For your use-case (transactional notifications) leaning towards 30s felt like a good tradeoff.
[04:04] Rita: can we do per-key TTLs? some templates are very stable, others not.
[04:08] Priya: yes, Redwood supports per-key TTL and also size-based eviction. you can configure a rule set: e.g., if template classified stable -> 5m TTL, otherwise 30s. we can help with classifier heuristics.
[04:20] Jordan: quick note about prompt reuse strategy - we recommend extracting a stable prefix (the instruction and template) and separating dynamic slots. then build the cache key from the canonicalized prefix + normalized slot placeholders. avoid including user IDs, timestamps, session tokens in the key.
[04:38] Alex: do you have examples of canonicalization?
[04:41] Priya: yes; e.g., trim whitespace, lowercase non-proper nouns, remove variable noise (uuid-like strings), canonicalize date formats to ISO, and for structured attributes map synonyms to a single key. We'll send a small cookbook.
[04:57] Leah: any gotchas when we canonicalize that could degrade quality?
[05:00] Priya: yes over-normalization can collapse semantically different prompts, e.g., removing 'express' vs 'standard' shipping might conflate intent. we suggest a conservative set of rules and evals on a held-out prompt set. Redwood Optimize (note: transcript sometimes says 'Optimise') can run prompt-level regression checks.
[05:20] Samir: what about memory sizing? we have budget limits on Dedicated nodes. if we keep a big pinned set, how do we model cost?
[05:28] Priya: we provided a sizing spreadsheet last week but short answer: memory scales linearly with average prefix length and number of entries. we can provide predicted memory usage for top 2k prefixes and recommended quantization/compression profiles. For example our test with 2k prefixes (avg prefix 480 bytes) used ~950MB of memory with small metadata overhead.
[05:50] Jordan: another practical: do we cache whole KV of key->kv-cache-prompt or store pre-tokenized prefix? we do both depending on runtime. storing tokenized prefix reduces CPU for tokenization but increases compatibility concerns across tokenizer/ model variants.
[06:10] Priya: definitely store tokenized prefix when model and tokenizer are stable; otherwise store canonical text and tokenize at runtime. for your pilot where model is pinned it's fine to use tokenized cache.
[06:22] Alex: any differences between Hosted and Dedicated behavior we should be aware of?
[06:27] Priya: hosted supports per-tenant cache but multi-tenant isolation means you don't get pinning guarantees; Dedicated gives you fine-grained control, pinning, reserved cache mem, and lower jitter. Private (VPC) adds customer KMS integration and audit logs for key derivation ops.
[06:45] Rita: latency SLA concerns - what p95 should we expect with caching?
[06:49] Priya: on hits p95 was about 110ms in our tests, on misses p95 around 420ms. your p95 overall depends on hit-rate mix. if you can get to 70% hit-rate overall p95 drops below ~200ms in our environment.
[07:06] Leah: we have to evaluate hallucination/regression risk - does caching change model outputs in ways we should monitor?
[07:12] Priya: caching only affects inference startup (prefix reuse) not model weights; the risk is if your canonicalization accidentally removes context that changes output. we recommend a regression suite and Redwood can tie quality alerts to specific prompts.
[07:28] Jordan: ok let's talk experiments - we'll run the 10k-prefix bench and provide CSV with hit-rate by prefix rank and latency columns, and we'll test pinning top-500 vs top-2k.
[07:40] Alex: can you also include a replay where dynamic slots are masked vs unmasked so we can measure delta?
[07:45] Priya: yes we'll add that as a second column in the CSV.
[07:50] Samir: security: please include redaction guidance for PHI and the hashing HMAC approach in the doc you send.
[07:56] Jordan: noted. We'll bundle SOC2 + KMS flow + network diagram with the benchmark results.
[08:03] Rita: timeline workable? we need results before next sprint planning (Dec 8).
[08:07] Jordan: target deliverables by Dec 7 so you can review prior to planning.
[08:12] Evan: i'll set a follow-up for Dec 9 to go over the CSV and decide pilot rollback criteria.
[08:18] Leah: one more thing - how do we instrument front-end so we can tag hits/misses and surface to our dashboards?
[08:23] Priya: we have a small SDK snippet that emits a cache-hit boolean and prefix-id to logs; we'll share instrumentation snippet and a Grafana dashboard template.
[08:33] Alex: perfect, that will help ops triage any user-facing regressions quickly.
[08:38] Jordan: any other q's?
[08:41] Rita: not from me, thanks everyone.
[08:43] Samir: none, thanks.
[08:45] Jordan: great recap: Redwood to run benchmark (10k prefixes, TTLs 5/30/120s), share CSV + SOC2/KMS docs by 2026-12-07; FinSettle to share prompt corpus + traffic distro by 2026-12-03; schedule canonicalization deep-dive week of 2026-12-08. Evan to schedule Dec 9 review. Thanks all.

End of transcript.
